scenario_provenance.archetype_label: Multi-focus on Practices 3 & 4 (analyze data; interpret results)
validity_rules: OBSERVATIONAL comparison only (no random assignment -> no causal claim)
means differ but spreads overlap so an over-strong claim is refutable

sources.note: the item stem's verb must match the scored demand

prompt: In a survey of eating habits, self-described high-fiber eaters had a mean daily satiety score of 49 points (SD about 12) and self-described low-fiber eaters had a mean of 45 points (SD about 12). A student claims: "self-described high-fiber eaters always have a higher daily satiety score than self-described low-fiber eaters." Which statement best justifies whether the data support this claim?

options.text: Since the mean for self-described high-fiber eaters (49) is greater than for self-described low-fiber eaters (45), every member of self-described high-fiber eaters must have a higher daily satiety score than every member of self-described low-fiber eaters.

misconception_source.label: Treated a difference in means as a claim about every individual value

sources.note: on-average differences must not be over-read as claims about all individual values; overlap matters

options.text: The claim is correct because self-described high-fiber eaters clearly did better on daily satiety score.

misconception_source.label: Restated the claim without citing statistical evidence

sources.ref: AP_STATISTICS_2027_CED_FACT_PACK.md S4/S6 (skill 4.B; task verbs) + S10 'General exam-wide conventions'
sources.note: a justification must reference the statistical evidence, not merely restate the claim

options.text: Because self-described high-fiber eaters had a higher mean daily satiety score, being in self-described high-fiber eaters causes a higher daily satiety score.

misconception_source.label: Interpreted an observational association as causation

sources.note: EK 5.2.A.4: correlation does not imply causation (stated explicitly)
observational studies (no random assignment) do not support causal claims

options.text: On average self-described high-fiber eaters had a higher daily satiety score (mean 49 vs 45), so the data support a typical difference; but because both SDs are about 12, the distributions overlap substantially, so the data do not support a claim that self-described high-fiber eaters are always higher.

parts.prompt: In a survey of eating habits, self-described high-fiber eaters had a mean daily satiety score of 49 points (SD about 12) and self-described low-fiber eaters had a mean of 45 points (SD about 12). A student claims: "self-described high-fiber eaters always have a higher daily satiety score than self-described low-fiber eaters." Which statement best justifies whether the data support this claim?

criteria.description: Selects the justification that affirms the on-average difference while rejecting the over-strong 'always' claim due to overlap.
